verses.text: Moses answered, “But, behold, they will not believe me, nor listen to my voice; for they will say, ‘Yahweh has not appeared to you.’”
Yahweh said to him, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A rod.”
He said, “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it on the ground, and it became a snake; and Moses ran away from it.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand, and take it by the tail.” He stretched out his hand, and took hold of it, and it became a rod in his hand.
“That they may believe that Yahweh, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
Yahweh said furthermore to him, “Now put your hand inside your cloak.” He put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous, as white as snow.
He said, “Put your hand inside your cloak again.” He put his hand inside his cloak again, and when he took it out of his cloak, behold, it had turned again as his other flesh.
“It will happen, if they will not believe you or listen to the voice of the first sign, that they will believe the voice of the latter sign.

It will happen, if they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, that you shall take of the water of the river, and pour it on the dry land. The water which you take out of the river will become blood on the dry land.”
Moses said to Yahweh, “O Lord,  I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”
Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
He said, “Oh, Lord, please send someone else.”

Yahweh’s anger burned against Moses, and he said, “What about Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Also, behold, he comes out to meet you. When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.
You shall speak to him, and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth, and with his mouth, and will teach you what you shall do.
He will be your spokesman to the people; and it will happen, that he will be to you a mouth, and you will be to him as God.
You shall take this rod in your hand, with which you shall do the signs.”

Moses went and returned to Jethro his father-in-law, and said to him, “Please let me go and return to my brothers who are in Egypt, and see whether they are still alive.” Jethro said to Moses, “Go in peace.”
Yahweh said to Moses in Midian, “Go, return into Egypt; for all the men who sought your life are dead.”
Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them on a donkey, and he returned to the land of Egypt. Moses took God’s rod in his hand.
Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.
You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Yahweh says, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
On the way at a lodging place, Yahweh met Moses and wanted to kill him.
Then Zipporah took a flint, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet; and she said, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me.”
So he let him alone. Then she said, “You are a bridegroom of blood,” because of the circumcision.
Yahweh said to Aaron, “Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.” He went, and met him on God’s mountain, and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all Yahweh’s words with which he had sent him, and all the signs with which he had instructed him.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the children of Israel.
Aaron spoke all the words which Yahweh had spoken to Moses, and did the signs in the sight of the people.
The people believed, and when they heard that Yahweh had visited the children of Israel, and that he had seen their affliction, then they bowed their heads and worshiped.

footnotes.content: Even standing face-to-face with the Lord, Moses doubts. He's already seen the burning bush, heard the Name—yet his first word is 'But.' How tenderly the Lord bears with us when we struggle to believe what we've just been promised. He never shames us for asking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A simple rod in an old shepherd's hand. The Lord doesn't ask Moses to become someone new—He asks him to look at what he already holds. Sometimes faith begins by recognizing what's already been given to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rod becomes a serpent, and Moses flees. Even the Lord's own signs can frighten us at first. The distance between trust and terror is sometimes just one moment of surprise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Catch it by the tail—the very part that made it dangerous. The Lord calls Moses not to run from the hard thing, but to face it directly. In His hands, what terrifies us becomes our instrument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sign points not to Moses' power, but to the Lord's faithfulness to their fathers. Every generation discovers the same God: the one Abraham trusted, the one Isaac knew, the one Jacob wrestled with. His character doesn't change.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A living hand suddenly becomes unclean, white as snow—yet when withdrawn again, it's whole. The Lord shows Moses that sickness and wholeness both rest in His hand. What He takes can be restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The second miracle reverses the first—from leprous back to whole. The Lord doubles His assurance to Moses in a way Moses can feel in his own body. Sometimes faith grows when we experience His power directly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If Israel doubts the first sign, they'll believe the second. The Lord prepares multiple witnesses—not out of meanness, but out of mercy. He knows how hard it is to trust, and He gives what's needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Water into blood—a sign terrible and unmistakable. The Lord warns of harder judgments to come, but offers them now as signs of His seriousness, not yet as punishment. He gives Israel room to choose belief before the plagues arrive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses tries one more objection: he's not a good speaker. It's an honest confession—and a very human one. So often we try to negotiate with the Lord by listing our shortcomings, as if He hadn't already seen them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who made the mouth? The Lord reminds Moses: *I* am the source of speech, silence, sight, blindness. Your weakness doesn't disqualify you—it shows me you understand where real power comes from.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will be with your mouth. The Lord doesn't fix Moses' stutter or make him eloquent—He offers something better: His presence. Sometimes being heard by God matters more than being eloquent to crowds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After signs, after reassurance, Moses still pleads: 'Send someone else.' The refusal comes not from doubt alone, but from a deep knowing of his own limits. We're not wrong to feel unequal to what the Lord calls us to do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's anger burned—but not in hatred. It's a father's frustration with a child who won't step forward. Yet even in that heat, He provides: Aaron, Moses' brother, already on his way. The Lord works around our resistance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You'll speak to Aaron; I'll be with both your mouths. The Lord honors Moses' weakness by giving him a helper. Partnership, not solo heroism—that's His design when we're afraid.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron becomes Moses' mouth; Moses becomes as God to Aaron. A tender image: each man carries what the other lacks. In the Lord's economy, mutual weakness becomes mutual strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take this rod—the one that turned to a serpent. You'll perform the signs with it. The instrument of Moses' fear becomes the instrument of Israel's deliverance. Nothing is wasted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses asks Jethro, his father-in-law, for leave to go check on his brothers in Egypt. Jethro blesses him with 'Go in peace'—a gentle release. Sometimes the Lord uses others to give us the permission we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Midian, far from the threat, the Lord reminds Moses: all your pursuers are dead. Forty years of safety had a purpose—not escape, but preparation. The timing of our calling follows God's patient reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses takes his wife, his sons, and the rod—all he loves, all he needs. The journey back to Egypt isn't an escape; it's an obedience that involves everyone he holds dear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wonders are in Moses' hand—yet Pharaoh's heart will be hardened. A hard truth: our faithfulness doesn't guarantee the outcome we want. The Lord's sovereignty and human choice both stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel is My son, My firstborn. The Lord claims Israel not as slaves to manage, but as sons to be freed. A revolutionary word: every captive bears the image of God's beloved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let My son go, that he may serve Me—or I will kill your son, your firstborn. A terrible symmetry: Pharaoh once killed Hebrew sons; now the Lord threatens his. Justice has a cost that reaches both high and low.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At a lodging place, the Lord met Moses and wanted to kill him. A shocking turn: the called servant faces judgment from the One who called him. Something in Moses' household is undone before his work can begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zipporah takes a flint and circumcises her son, casting the foreskin at Moses' feet. She speaks: 'You are a bridegroom of blood to me.' A covenant act, done by a faithful woman when the man wavers between worlds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord lets Moses alone. Zipporah's quick obedience—her willingness to seal the covenant on their son—turns away the judgment. Sometimes the faithfulness of one person shields another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord tells Aaron to go meet Moses in the wilderness. Aaron goes and meets him at God's mountain and kisses him. Two brothers, sent by the Lord toward each other, meet with embrace. The provision arrives exactly when needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses tells Aaron all the Lord's words and all the signs. He shares what he knows—not what he understands fully, but what he's been given. Aaron listens, and together they can move forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and Aaron gather the elders of Israel. The Word moves from the Lord to Moses to Aaron to the gathered people. Truth travels by a chain of faithful transmission, each link strengthening the next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron speaks the words and performs the signs. Moses' weakness and Aaron's mouth combine. The signs aren't empty wonders—they're proof that the Lord has been at work all along.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people believed when they heard that the Lord had visited Israel and seen their affliction. Readers today hear an echo: the Lord still sees, still comes near to those bowed under burden. What drew Israel's faith then draws ours still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
